title: Enemies
tomorrow: in Jesus' story the poor man has a name. the rich man doesn't. why?

lines: A ONE-STAR REVIEW, YOUR NAME IN IT.
cards: A one-star review with your name in it. A group chat that goes quiet when you walk in. Someone who did real harm and never said sorry.
Praying for them can feel impossible, or fake. So is there a way to pray for someone you can't stand yet? Jesus' command has a step in it built for exactly that.

teach.b: Here's the whole verse: “Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.” Notice the last step. Warm feelings can take years.
Doing good may not be safe, or possible. But prayer is open to someone who can't yet manage a kind word.

teach.h: HIS SUN ON THE EVIL AND THE GOOD.
teach.b: Jesus gives the reason in the next line: “That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good.”
And he does it himself; on the cross he prays, “Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.” Now a neighbor who says it too.

teach.h: A NEIGHBOR: HATRED CEASES BY LOVE.
teach.b: The Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings, reads in Max Müller's translation: “For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule.”
The same instinct: hate answered with hate only grows. And one honest difference.

teach.h: THE FATHER, OR AN OLD RULE.
teach.b: Jesus grounds it in God: be like the Father, whose sun rises on everyone, and pray. The Dhammapada calls it an old rule, a law of how hatred works, with no prayer to God in the verse.
Two neighbors refusing the same cycle, each for their own reasons. And none of this means pretending harm was fine, or staying near someone who hurts you.
If anyone is in danger, getting safe comes first: local emergency help, and someone you trust.

how: Some Christians pray for an enemy by name, even briefly, as Jesus commands in Matthew 5:44; Buddhists recite the Dhammapada's teaching that hatred ceases by love, and some practice loving-kindness toward those who have harmed them.

o: rival teams or schools you compete against for fun
people who've harmed or hate us, whom Jesus says to pray for
the forces of evil that tempt people to do wrong

games.q: the hardest command, two neighbors — tap the pairs.
p: rises on the evil and on the good

s: loving enemies means pretending the harm was fine
it never means calling a wrong right, or staying near someone who hurts you.
Matthew gives a reason: the Father's sun rises on the evil and on the good
"That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven."
the Dhammapada's line and Jesus' command are the same teaching
both answer hatred with love. Jesus grounds it in the Father and prayer; the Dhammapada calls it an old rule.

games.q: a classmate spread a lie about you last month. you're not ready to be friendly. what step does Matthew 5:44 leave open?
o: act like nothing happened, starting today.
pray for them, even before the feeling comes.
wait until you feel love before doing anything.
games.why: Jesus' list ends with pray for them. prayer is open to someone who can't yet manage a kind word.

practice: On paper, write the first name or just the initial of someone you can't stand yet. Under it, write the one thing you can manage today: pray for them, or simply, I don't wish them harm.
Fold the paper, hold it through the sit, and let the feeling be whatever it is.

wordCard.voice: Enemies. The people who've harmed us or hate us, and the hardest command about them: love, bless, do good, pray.

orig.note: Greek: enemies, in 'love your enemies', Matthew 5:44.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: pray for them, the one step open even before the feeling comes. Day seventeen-twenty-one.
